title: Failure modes: timeouts, partial failure, cascades, thundering herd

claims.text: Dean and Barroso argue that software techniques tolerating latency variability are vital to building responsive large-scale services, drawing an analogy to fault-tolerant computing: just as fault tolerance creates a reliable whole from less-reliable parts, large online services need to create a predictably responsive whole out of less-predictable parts, which they call latency tail-tolerant.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, The tail at scale, Communications of the ACM 56(2):74-80, February 2013, doi 10.1145/2408776.2408794

claims.text: Their arithmetic of fan-out is the central point. If a single server has a 99th percentile latency of one second — a one in a hundred chance of being slow — then a request that fans out to 100 servers will see that slow response more often than not. With fan-out to 2,000 servers, even a one in ten thousand chance of a slow response means 18% of requests exceed one second.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, The tail at scale, Communications of the ACM 56(2):74-80, February 2013, doi 10.1145/2408776.2408794

claims.text: Their conclusion is that simply stamping out all sources of performance variability will not achieve responsiveness as systems scale up. Among the mitigations described are hedged requests — sending the same request to several replicas, taking the first response and cancelling the rest — with the refinement of adding a delay before issuing the second request, because cancellation messages often arrive after processing has begun and the naive form adds significant surplus load.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, The tail at scale, Communications of the ACM 56(2):74-80, February 2013, doi 10.1145/2408776.2408794

beats.broke: a component that is nearly always fast is not nearly always fast enough, because a request that depends on many components is exposed to the worst of them rather than the average
beats.fix: treat variability as a permanent property to be tolerated rather than a defect to be removed — bound every wait, degrade rather than fail, and where latency matters more than load, ask more than one replica and take the first answer
beats.cost: the tolerations cost work: a bounded wait abandons responses that would have arrived, and duplicate requests buy latency with load, which is exactly the resource that was scarce when things were slow
beats.interview: why a service whose slow responses are rare can still be slow almost every time
